subject: Dealing with too many zeroes in the response

messages.author: 6445c6a7b4eb1c70
messages.subject: Dealing with too many zeroes in the response
parts:
I'm currently working with quantitative response data that shows the viral load for each of several different strains of a particular virus in a sample of people (sort of like different variants of COVID-19). The problem is that the vast majority of people in my sample were not infected with any of the strains, so I have about 95% zeroes for each of the responses.

Is there a way to address this? Right now, I get the feeling that the sheer number of zeroes is masking any underlying relationships between predictor and response variables, but I'm not in a position to collect more data. The goal is to evaluate risk factors associated with these virus strains, and since the virus has a relatively low prevalence in most communities, these data are about as good as I'm going to get :)

messages.author: 5b9c62b1c7cbc1e6
messages.subject: Re: Dealing with too many zeroes in the response
parts:
Look into "hurdle" models.

You effectively have two outcome variables: COVID y/n, observed for everyone, and viral load which is missing (at random) when COVID=no. These variables can have different relations to predictors.

Pat

Y0 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + ... + Xn
